title: Week 101 · Lesson 125: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy — FNP-Level Recognition, Triage & Longitudinal Safety
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 101 — Lesson 125: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

FNP-level goal: Recognize pregnancy-related hypertension early, distinguish chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, and postpartum disease, identify severe features, coordinate evidence-based prevention and surveillance, and never allow a normal-looking patient or a single reassuring test to delay urgent care.

Learning Objectives

  • Classify hypertension by timing, prior history, blood-pressure pattern, proteinuria, organ dysfunction, and postpartum context.
  • Explain how abnormal placentation, endothelial dysfunction, vasospasm, and organ hypoperfusion produce maternal and fetal disease.
  • Perform a focused symptom, medication, blood-pressure, laboratory, and fetal-risk assessment.
  • Use risk factors to support current low-dose aspirin prevention decisions in collaboration with prenatal care.
  • Recognize severe hypertension, neurologic symptoms, pulmonary edema, hepatic injury, thrombocytopenia, fetal concern, and postpartum preeclampsia as urgent or emergency problems.

Part 1 — Classification Begins With Timing

Chronic hypertension predates pregnancy, is identified before 20 weeks, or persists beyond the expected postpartum transition. Gestational hypertension develops after 20 weeks without the proteinuria or end-organ findings that define preeclampsia. Preeclampsia is a multisystem disorder after 20 weeks characterized by new hypertension with proteinuria or specific maternal organ dysfunction; proteinuria is not required when qualifying severe features are present. Chronic hypertension with new proteinuria, worsening pressure, organ dysfunction, or other new preeclamptic findings raises concern for superimposed preeclampsia.

Postpartum disease matters. Preeclampsia and severe hypertension may first appear after birth. Any clinician seeing a patient during the first year after pregnancy should ask about recent pregnancy, but headache, visual change, dyspnea, chest pain, epigastric or right-upper-quadrant pain, seizure, or severe blood pressure in the early postpartum period demands especially rapid action.

Part 2 — Mechanism Explains the Organ Pattern

Abnormal placental vascular development and maternal endothelial dysfunction can increase vascular resistance, capillary leak, platelet activation, and organ hypoperfusion. The brain may manifest severe headache, visual symptoms, hyperreflexia, altered mental status, or seizure. The liver may produce right-upper-quadrant or epigastric pain and elevated transaminases. The kidneys may show rising creatinine or proteinuria. Capillary leak and cardiac strain may cause pulmonary edema. Placental insufficiency may contribute to fetal growth restriction, abnormal surveillance, abruption, or preterm delivery.

HELLP—hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets—is a dangerous phenotype within the preeclampsia spectrum. Blood pressure may not tell the whole story. A pregnant or postpartum patient with concerning symptoms and laboratory abnormalities needs obstetric-level evaluation even if the initial pressure is not dramatically high.

Part 3 — Blood-Pressure Technique Is a Safety Intervention

Use a validated device, correct cuff size, supported arm, appropriate position, rest, and repeated measurements. Confirm an unexpected reading without delaying emergency escalation when severe symptoms or instability are present. Review home-device technique and compare the device with office measurement when possible. Document gestational age, repeat values, symptoms, and who received the result.

A severe-range measurement is not managed as a routine portal message. Follow current obstetric protocols for confirmation and urgent treatment because sustained severe hypertension increases risk of stroke and other maternal injury. Never advise a symptomatic patient to drive themselves while repeatedly checking pressure at home.

Part 4 — Focused History and Examination

Ask about gestational age, prior pressures, previous preeclampsia, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, autoimmune disease, multifetal pregnancy, fertility treatment, family history, current medicines, aspirin use when prescribed, adherence, access, and recent obstetric findings. Assess headache character, visual symptoms, chest pain, dyspnea, orthopnea, edema trajectory, severe nausea or vomiting, right-upper-quadrant or epigastric pain, vaginal bleeding, contractions, fluid leakage, and change in fetal movement.

Examine general appearance, repeated blood pressure, oxygenation when indicated, mental and neurologic status, cardiopulmonary findings, edema in context, abdominal tenderness, and signs of alternative diagnoses. Do not dismiss a severe headache as migraine without considering pregnancy-related hypertension, cerebral vascular disease, infection, medication effects, and other secondary causes.

Part 5 — Diagnostics Answer Maternal and Fetal Questions

Urgency determines setting. Evaluation may include CBC with platelets, creatinine, hepatic studies, urine protein assessment, hemolysis evaluation when indicated, and fetal assessment according to gestational age and presentation. A normal urine dipstick does not exclude preeclampsia, and laboratory values can evolve. Serial clinical assessment matters when symptoms persist or the disease trajectory changes.

The fetus is part of the assessment. Growth, fluid, placental function, and antenatal surveillance may be relevant, but these decisions belong within the obstetric plan. The FNP should recognize incomplete follow-up, obtain missing records, and close referrals rather than independently improvising fetal surveillance.

Part 6 — Prevention and Longitudinal Risk

Current guidance supports low-dose aspirin after 12 weeks for patients at high risk of preeclampsia and may support it when multiple moderate-risk factors are present. This is a risk-based prenatal decision, not a universal over-the-counter recommendation. Review allergy, bleeding context, gestational timing, other medicines, and the obstetric plan. High-risk factors include prior preeclampsia, multifetal gestation, chronic hypertension, pregestational diabetes, kidney disease, and autoimmune disease; combinations of moderate-risk factors also matter.

Manage chronic hypertension with pregnancy-appropriate therapy and coordinated monitoring. Do not abruptly stop needed medication or continue a potentially unsafe regimen without review. The plan must identify blood-pressure goals under current guidance, maternal labs, fetal surveillance, medication monitoring, and who responds to out-of-range home readings.

Part 7 — Differential Diagnosis

Consider chronic or gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, superimposed preeclampsia, medication or stimulant effect, pain, anxiety, white-coat effect, kidney disease, thyroid disease, primary headache disorders, cerebral venous thrombosis, stroke, reversible posterior encephalopathy, hepatic or gallbladder disease, pulmonary embolism, cardiomyopathy, and infection. The purpose of the differential is to prevent anchoring—not to postpone obstetric evaluation in a high-risk presentation.

Part 8 — FNP Management Boundaries

Stable chronic hypertension may involve shared primary-care and obstetric management, medication reconciliation, adherence support, home monitoring, and cardiovascular-risk counseling. New gestational hypertension or suspected preeclampsia requires prompt obstetric coordination and a clearly documented surveillance and delivery plan. Severe features, acute neurologic symptoms, respiratory compromise, seizure, instability, concerning bleeding, or fetal-movement change require emergency or labor-and-delivery evaluation.

After pregnancy, ensure blood-pressure reassessment, medication review for lactation and long-term use, contraception and future-pregnancy counseling, transition to primary care, and cardiovascular-risk follow-up. A history of preeclampsia is not erased at the postpartum visit; it identifies increased later-life cardiovascular risk.

Clinical Case 1 — New Hypertension Without Symptoms

A patient at 31 weeks has repeated readings above the normal range but feels well and has no known chronic hypertension. The FNP repeats measurement correctly, assesses symptoms and fetal movement, reviews prior records, and arranges same-day obstetric guidance and appropriate laboratory/fetal evaluation. The absence of symptoms does not make new pregnancy hypertension routine.

Clinical Case 2 — Severe Features

A patient at 35 weeks has severe blood pressure, persistent headache, visual spots, and right-upper-quadrant pain. The priority is immediate obstetric emergency evaluation and safe transfer—not outpatient laboratory ordering followed by a next-day call.

Clinical Case 3 — Postpartum Headache

Ten days after delivery, a patient reports a worsening headache, shortness of breath, and facial swelling. The FNP explicitly identifies the recent pregnancy, checks immediate stability, and directs emergency evaluation for postpartum preeclampsia and cardiopulmonary complications. A completed delivery does not end pregnancy-related risk.

FNP High-Yield Framework: PRESS

  1. P — Pregnancy timing: gestational age, prior hypertension, delivery date, and postpartum interval.
  2. R — Repeat correctly: validated device, cuff, position, symptoms, and severe-range protocol.
  3. E — End-organ screen: brain, lungs, liver, kidneys, platelets, placenta, and fetus.
  4. S — Stratify and share care: chronic, gestational, preeclampsia, superimposed disease, prevention, and obstetric ownership.
  5. S — Safety disposition: routine co-management, same-day obstetric assessment, or emergency transfer.

Take-Home Summary

Pregnancy-related hypertension is a dynamic multisystem disorder. Timing classifies the syndrome; symptoms and organ findings define urgency; normal protein testing does not rule out severe disease. FNP-level care combines accurate measurement, rapid recognition, prevention, obstetric coordination, postpartum surveillance, and long-term cardiovascular follow-up.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace current ACOG/USPSTF guidance, local obstetric protocols, maternal-fetal medicine consultation, or emergency evaluation. Severe blood pressure, seizure, focal neurologic symptoms, persistent severe headache, visual change, chest pain, dyspnea, pulmonary edema, severe abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, or reduced fetal movement requires urgent assessment.
